tier_reason: The README cites the peer-reviewed SC '23 paper (Fu et al., 'PanguLU: A Scalable Regular Two-Dimensional Block-Cyclic Sparse Direct Solver on Distributed Heterogeneous Systems'), and a search result quoting its abstract gives up to 11.70x (128 A100) and 17.97x (128 MI50) over SuperLU_DIST. The paper itself could not be opened (dl.acm.org and sc23.supercomputing.org are egress-blocked), so B rests on the venue plus the abstract, per earlier precedents.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Peer-reviewed SC '23 paper, per its abstract as quoted in search results: on two distributed heterogeneous platforms with 128 NVIDIA A100 and 128 AMD MI50 GPUs, PanguLU achieves up to 11.70x and 17.97x speedups over SuperLU_DIST, and scales up to 47.51x and 74.84x over a single GPU. Paper body not opened.
corrections.caveats: Paper not opened (dl.acm.org, sc23.supercomputing.org, arxiv.org and researchgate.net are blocked here) and the README has no performance numbers, so the SuperLU_DIST version, matrices, typical (not maximum) speedups, compiler and flags are unverified. The figures are 'up to' maxima from a 2023 version (v3.x era); the code is now v5.0.0. Distributed multi-GPU result (MPI + OpenMP + CUDA), so single-node CPU users may see very different ratios. SuperLU_DIST is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc baseline list (PETSc can call it). AGPL-3.0 is OSI-approved but strong copyleft, including network use.

notes: Repo page: AGPL-3.0, 51 stars, 15 forks, not archived, 38 commits. The commits page heads its latest commit 'v5.0.0' with 'Commits on Jun 25, 2026', while the README dates v5.0.0 to Jul. 31, 2025; I used the commit date, which makes the project active rather than stale.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (qpsolvers/qpbenchmark v2.3.0, run by its maintainer on a stated i7-6500U, public harness, solver versions listed) shows PIQP ahead of OSQP on runtime shifted geometric mean at all four settings with a 73-97% success rate; it runs prebuilt Python wheels, so no compiler or flags exist and it falls short of A. Also backed by the peer-reviewed CDC 2023 paper (doi 10.1109/CDC49753.2023.10383915) cited in the README.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0 (2024-09-07), Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean with PIQP = 1.0: OSQP 12.7 (default), 16.1 (high accuracy), 52.8 (low), 51.9 (mid); sparse subset (76 problems): OSQP 9.5 / 17.4 / 30.0 / 56.0. Success rates on the full set: PIQP 95.7 / 73.2 / 97.1 / 94.2% vs OSQP 43.5 / 26.1 / 21.0 / 24.6%. First-party piqp_benchmarks on Maros-Meszaros (shifted geometric means, PIQP = 1.0): OSQP 7.55 at low accuracy (eps_abs 1e-3, eps_rel 1e-4) and 42.66 at high accuracy (eps_abs 1e-8, eps_rel 1e-9).
corrections.caveats: Category fit is loose: PIQP is a convex QP optimization solver (header-only C++14 on Eigen), not a sparse linear-system solver, and OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc baseline list; there is no optimization-solver category in this wave. The qpbenchmark run used prebuilt Python wheels (piqp 0.4.1, osqp 0.6.7.post0, qpsolvers 4.3.3, Python 3.12), so no compiler or flags apply, runtimes include a sliver of wrapper time, and the versions are two years old (PIQP is now 0.6.x). The suite's known limitations include CPU thermal throttling (issue 88) on a 2-core laptop CPU. Only solves that return no solution are counted at the 1000 s time limit (qpbenchmark/results.py not_found_value); solutions returned as solved but failing the tolerance check keep their measured runtime. Rankings depend on the suite: ProxQP's own benchmark (different problem classes) shows ProxQP ahead of OSQP instead.

notes: All qpbenchmark numbers match results/maros_meszaros.md and maros_meszaros_sparse.md; piqp_benchmarks numbers and Threadripper 3990X match its README. Repo: BSD-2-Clause, 149 stars, 23 forks, not a fork, latest commit 2026-08-28 ('prepare 0.6.4 release'). Category: QP solver compared with OSQP, off the sparse-and-solvers baseline list.

tier_reason: Independent third-party suite (qpsolvers/qpbenchmark v2.3.0 on a stated i7-6500U, public harness, solver versions listed) shows QPALM's runtime shifted geometric mean below OSQP's at all four settings; prebuilt Python wheels mean no compiler or flags, so B rather than A. The README also points to its arXiv papers (1911.02934, 2010.02653) for benchmarks; those were not opened (arxiv.org blocked).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0 (2024-09-07), Maros-Meszaros (138 problems), runtime shifted geometric mean (best solver = 1.0, which is PIQP): QPALM 3.6 vs OSQP 12.7 (default), 4.8 vs 16.1 (high accuracy), 3.4 vs 52.8 (low), 2.2 vs 51.9 (mid). Sparse subset (76 problems): QPALM 3.2 vs OSQP 9.5, 4.3 vs 17.4, 3.1 vs 30.0, 1.8 vs 56.0. Success rates on the full set: QPALM 55.8 / 25.4 / 31.2 / 31.2% vs OSQP 43.5 / 26.1 / 21.0 / 24.6%; on the sparse subset QPALM 53 / 8 / 11 / 13% vs OSQP 37 / 13 / 7 / 11%. QPALM's 'solved' return codes were correct on only 57 / 63 / 34 / 37% of problems (full set).
corrections.caveats: The runtime advantage is weakly supported outside default settings: qpbenchmark charges the 1000 s time limit only when a solver returns no solution (qpbenchmark/results.py not_found_value), so QPALM's frequent 'solved' answers that fail the tolerance check (return codes correct on only 34-37% of problems at low/mid accuracy) are timed at face value, and its success rate at high/low/mid accuracy is only 25-31% (8-13% on the sparse subset, below OSQP at high accuracy). Its duality-gap shifted geometric mean is very poor (1237362.9 at high accuracy). Category fit is loose: QP optimization solver, not a linear-system solver; OSQP is not in the SuiteSparse/Eigen/PETSc list. Prebuilt Python wheels (qpalm 1.2.3, osqp 0.6.7.post0), so no compiler or flags; the suite's known limitations include CPU thermal throttling. QPALM is itself about 2-5x slower than PIQP in the same table. The QPALM repo has no numbers of its own; it points to two arXiv papers that were not opened. LGPL-3.0 core; bundled LADEL and LOBPCG are LGPL-3.0 and LAPACK is BSD-3.

notes: Numbers in the record match both qpbenchmark pages, but the record omitted that QPALM's success rate and return-code correctness are poor at non-default tolerances; shortcoming worth recording: QPALM often reports 'solved' for solutions that fail the tolerance check. Repo page shows it is forked from Benny44/QPALM_vLADEL (the kul-optec repo is the maintained one); LGPL-3.0, 32 stars, 5 forks, latest commit 2026-08-26 ('Version 1.3.0').
